source_refs.note: Book p. 218: 12.1.1, sequence x_n = 1/n^2 tending to 0. Book errors: listed values 1, 1/2, 1/2^2, ..., 1/2^n (should be 1, 1/4, 1/9, ..., 1/n^2); 'x' for x_n; 'as n -> 0' (should be n -> infinity). Teaching notes are ours.

items.title: 12.1.1 Meaning of the Phrase "x approaches zero" (Roman Urdu)

blocks.text: Chaliye pehla jumla samajhte hain: "x approaches zero". Kitab yeh baat ek sequence (silsila) ki madad se samjhati hai. Sequence kya hai? Numbers ki ek tarteeb wali list: pehla term, doosra term, teesra term, aur yun hi aage. Rule \(x_{n} = \frac{1}{n^{2}}\) humein \(n\)-wan term deta hai. Asal mein sequence ek function hi hai jis ka input sirf natural numbers \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) hote hain.

Kitab kehti hai: farz karein sequence \(x_{n} = \frac{1}{n^{2}}\) yeh values leta hai:
\[1, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{9}, \frac{1}{16}, \ldots, \frac{1}{n^{2}}, \ldots\]

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text:
Kitab yahan \(1, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2^{2}}, \frac{1}{2^{3}}, \ldots, \frac{1}{2^{n}}\) chhaapti hai. Yeh \(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\) ki values nahin, balke \(\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}\) ki values hain. Khud check kijiye: \(n = 2\) rakhein to \(\frac{1}{2^{2}} = \frac{1}{4}\) aata hai, \(\frac{1}{2}\) nahin. Is liye hum ne upar sahi values likhi hain: \(1, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{9}, \frac{1}{16}, \ldots\)
Achhi baat yeh hai ke dono sequences zero ki taraf hi jaati hain, is liye sabaq ka asal khayal nahin badalta.

blocks.caption: Hamari table (kitab mein nahin): jaise jaise n bara hota hai, x_n = 1/n^2 ke terms 0 ki taraf sukarte jaate hain.

blocks.text: Table ko ooper se neeche parhiye. \(n\) ko 10 guna kiya (10 se 100, 100 se 1000) to term 100 guna chhota ho gaya, kyun ke denominator mein \(n\) ka square hai. Terms bohat tezi se zero ki taraf bhaag rahe hain, lekin har term phir bhi ek positive number hai. Yeh dono baatein ek saath yaad rakhiye: qareeb se qareeb tar, magar kabhi barabar nahin.

Ab kitab ki agli baat. Hum dekh sakte hain ke jaise jaise \(n\) barhta hai, \(x_{n}\) chhota aur chhota hota jata hai, aur \(n\) ko kaafi bara le kar hum use jitna chahein chhota bana sakte hain. Doosre lafzon mein, \(n\) bara hone ke saath \(x_{n} = \frac{1}{n^{2}}\) zero ke qareeb se qareeb tar hota jata hai.

\(x_{n}\) ki is kabhi na khatam hone wali kami (unending decrease) ko \(x_{n} \to 0\) likhte hain aur parhte hain "\(x_{n}\) approaches zero" ya "\(x_{n}\) tends to zero as \(n \to \infty\)". Yani sequence \(x_{n}\) ki limit \(0\) hai.

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text:
1. Kitab pehle jumle mein sirf \(x\) likhti hai; murad sequence ke terms \(x_{n}\) hain.
2. Kitab "tends to zero as \(n \to 0\)" chhaapti hai. Sahi "as \(n \to \infty\)" hai. Kyun? Terms is liye chhote ho rahe hain ke \(n\) bara ho raha hai, is liye nahin ke \(n\) zero ke qareeb ja raha hai. Ulta, agar \(n\) zero ke qareeb hota to \(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\) behad bara ho jata. Hum ne upar sahi likha hai.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
"Jitna chahein chhota" (as small as we please) ka asal matlab kya hai? Matlab yeh: aap koi bhi chhota sa positive number bata dein, aik waqt aayega ke us ke baad saare terms us se bhi chhote honge.
Misal: hum chahte hain \(x_{n} < 0.0001\) ho.
\[\frac{1}{n^{2}} < \frac{1}{10000}\]
\[\Leftrightarrow n^{2} > 10000\]
\[\Leftrightarrow n > 100\]
Kyun: fraction ka numerator 1 hai, to fraction tab chhota hoga jab denominator bara ho; isi liye inequality ulat kar \(n^{2} > 10000\) ho gayi, aur dono taraf square root lene se \(n > 100\).
Yani 100ve term ke baad har term \(0.0001\) se chhota hai. Agar target \(0.000001\) ho to \(n > 1000\) lena hoga. Target jitna bhi chhota ho, koi na koi \(n\) mil jata hai. Yahi "zero ki taraf jaane" ka sahi matlab hai.

blocks.title: Dhyan dein
blocks.text: Koi bhi term kabhi bilkul \(0\) nahin hota, kyun ke har \(n\) ke liye \(\frac{1}{n^{2}} > 0\) hai. Ek positive number ko kisi bhi positive number se divide karein, jawab positive hi rahega. To limit \(0\) woh value hai jis ki taraf terms ja rahe hain, woh value nahin jis tak woh pohanch jaate hain.

blocks.title: Khud sochiye
blocks.text:
Sequence \(y_{n} = \frac{1}{10^{n}}\) ke pehle chaar terms likhiye. Kya yeh bhi zero ko approach karta hai? \(y_{n} < 0.00001\) ke liye \(n\) kitna hona chahiye?
Jawab: \(0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, \ldots\); haan, \(y_{n} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\). Aur \(\frac{1}{10^{n}} < \frac{1}{10^{5}}\) tab hoga jab \(n > 5\), yani chhatay term se aage.

blocks.title: Hamari taraf se misaal
blocks.text:
Ek roti ko socho. Pehle din aap aadhi kha lete hain, doosre din baqi ka aadha, teesre din phir baqi ka aadha... Baqi roti: \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{8}, \ldots\)
Har din baqi hissa chhota hota jata hai aur zero ke qareeb jata hai, lekin kisi din bilkul khatam nahin hota. Bas yahi \(x_{n} \to 0\) ki tasveer hai.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Definition wale sawal mein poora jumla likhiye: "\(x_{n} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\)", yani "\(x_{n}\) tends to zero as \(n\) tends to infinity". Dono teer zaroori hain: ek batata hai terms kya kar rahe hain, doosra batata hai \(n\) kya kar raha hai. Examiner aksar sirf ek teer likhne par number kaat leta hai.

blocks.title: Yaad rakhne wali baatein
blocks.text:
1. \(x_{n} = \frac{1}{n^{2}}\) se \(1, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{9}, \frac{1}{16}, \ldots\) milte hain: terms be-inteha (without end) chhote hote jaate hain.
2. \(n\) kaafi bara lein to terms kisi bhi positive number se chhote ho jaate hain, lekin kabhi zero nahin hote.
3. Is ko likhte hain \(x_{n} \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\): "\(x_{n}\) approaches zero"; sequence ki limit \(0\) hai.
4. Sequence ek aisa function hai jis ka input sirf natural numbers hain.

blocks.title: Aam ghaltiyan
blocks.text:
1. "as \(n \to 0\)" likh dena, jaisa kitab mein ghalti se chhapa hai. Sequence mein \(n\) hamesha \(\infty\) ki taraf jata hai.
2. Yeh samajhna ke sirf "chhota hota ja raha hai" ka matlab "zero ki taraf" hai. Sequence \(1 + \frac{1}{n}\) ke terms bhi chhote hote jaate hain (\(2, 1.5, 1.33, 1.25, \ldots\)), lekin woh \(1\) ki taraf jaate hain, \(0\) ki taraf nahin. Asal sharat yeh hai ke terms \(0\) ke jitna chahein qareeb aa jayein.
3. Yeh sochna ke koi term aakhir kaar bilkul \(0\) ban jayega. \(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\) kabhi zero nahin hota.
